# Safety and Privacy

Yantra keeps browser automation inside explicit boundaries: model-visible data is masked or sanitized, stored secrets resolve only at an execution boundary, classified high-risk actions require consent, outbound work is policy-checked, and each created run leaves a local audit trail. These controls are enforced by the runtime rather than relying only on model instructions.

## What It Does

### The boundary at a glance

| Data or action                                  | Model sees                                                                      | Execution boundary sees                                              | Persisted form                                                                              |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Explicitly marked run input                     | A token such as `{{user:password:1}}`                                           | The original value only when a validated tool parameter is executed  | Placeholder or neutral text; not the original value                                         |
| Keychain-backed website secret                  | The secret reference key, never its value                                       | The value after consent and a live-host check                        | Reference key and resolution outcome only                                                   |
| Third-party page or document content            | Profile-sanitized, size-bounded content                                         | The page content needed by the operation                             | Sanitized captures and tool projections; the provider session is a sensitive local artifact |
| A value the model supplied itself               | The value remains visible                                                       | The validated tool receives it                                       | Sanitized tool projection                                                                   |
| Password, one-time-code, or payment field state | `value_present: true`, a `withheld` reason, and after a fill an in-page verdict | The browser fill path can set the value and check it inside the page | No protected value in the tool result, trace, or other run artifact                         |
| Protected click or stored-secret fill           | A confirmation result and opaque confirmation id                                | The operation only after a human grant                               | Request, decision, provenance, and linkage to the tool call                                 |
| Saved screenshot (`browser_capture`)            | Its path, dimensions, byte size, and labels; never pixels or a hash             | The page's pixels, refused while a stored secret is latched          | Owner-only PNG under `screenshots/`; metadata-only reference with `sent_to_model: false`    |

Marked input and keychain secrets solve different problems. A marker is a run-scoped privacy boundary; it is not a credential store, trusted-host binding, or request for confirmation. A keychain-backed website secret adds durable storage, trusted-host checking, and mandatory confirmation.

### Explicit user-input masking

In a model-backed `do`, `ask`, or `research` run, wrap any value that must stay out of the model in `@{...}` or a tagged form:

```bash
yantra do 'log into xyz.com as @username{u1} with @password{p1}'
```

Yantra parses markers before creating a run directory or provider session. It replaces each marked value with a stable placeholder, resolves that placeholder only inside a validated tool call, and masks echoed values back to the same placeholder before results return to the model. The raw marked value is excluded from run artifacts and promoted workflow YAML.

The marker grammar is:

<!-- parser-example: {"input":"@{demo-value}","segments":[{"kind":"value","tag":"secret","value":"demo-value"}]} -->
<!-- parser-example: {"input":"@password{demo-value}","segments":[{"kind":"value","tag":"password","value":"demo-value"}]} -->
<!-- parser-example: {"input":"@{a{b}c}","segments":[{"kind":"value","tag":"secret","value":"a{b}c"}]} -->
<!-- parser-example: {"input":"@{{\"mode\":\"demo\"}}","segments":[{"kind":"value","tag":"secret","value":"{\"mode\":\"demo\"}"}]} -->
<!-- parser-example: {"input":"@{p\\}1}","segments":[{"kind":"value","tag":"secret","value":"p}1"}]} -->
<!-- parser-example: {"input":"@@{x}","segments":[{"kind":"literal","text":"@{x}"}]} -->

| Form             | Meaning                                   | Example                 |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| `@{value}`       | Generic protected value, tagged `secret`  | `@{demo-value}`         |
| `@tag{value}`    | Protected value with a closed tag         | `@password{demo-value}` |
| Balanced braces  | Nested braces belong to the same value    | `@{a{b}c}`              |
| `\{`, `\}`, `\\` | Literal brace or backslash inside a value | `@{p\}1}`               |
| `@@`             | Literal `@`; opt out of marker parsing    | `@@{not-protected}`     |

Allowed public tags are `secret`, `username`, `password`, `pin`, `otp`, `national_id`, `vin`, `account`, `dob`, `address`, `email`, `phone`, `ssn`, `credit_card`, and `api_key`. `auth_param` is internal-only. Marker bodies must contain 1–2048 characters and cannot be whitespace-only. Unknown tags, unterminated markers, oversized or empty values, and user-written `{{user:...}}` placeholders are validation errors.

Malformed markers exit with code `1` before a run, browser, or provider session exists. The error identifies the 1-based column without echoing the protected value.

Markers are the guarantee within Yantra's model-and-artifact boundary. English keyword look-around and shape detectors for recognizable email, phone, SSN, Luhn-valid card, API-key, authenticated-query, and checksum-valid VIN forms add best-effort protection for unmarked input. They intentionally avoid guessing every national identifier, username, account number, or password. If a value matters, mark it.

### Sanitization profiles and contextual scope

Every model-visible tool result is masked, passed through a declared sanitization profile, and byte-bounded by mandatory middleware. A tool cannot opt out at call time.

| Profile          | What reaches the model                                                                                               | Action boundary                                                              |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `public`         | Form values and common PII/credential shapes are redacted; authentication-shaped query parameters are stripped       | Normal public-web operations                                                 |
| `read-only-data` | Real values may be sent to the model so it can summarize them; output is still capped at 20 KB by the core sanitizer | Preflight permits only `extract`, `wait_for`, and `llm_summarize` plan steps |
| `authenticated`  | Form values, all query strings, and common PII/credential shapes are redacted                                        | Used for authenticated and credential-adjacent results                       |

Source-attributed sanitization can also apply packaged low-false-positive redactors for banking, brokerage, credit, health, government, payroll/tax, and auto-insurance hosts—for example account, IBAN, member, medical-record, tax, passport, driver's-license, VIN, date-of-birth, case-number, and currency patterns.

The `read-only-data` profile is an intentional disclosure mode, not a stronger redaction profile. Its safety property is the static no-mutation scope. A plan that puts any other step type in that scope is rejected before execution.

### Structural sanitization of audited tool payloads

Tool inputs and outputs that cross the provider-session seam into the session audit (the `tool-calls.jsonl` projection) are sanitized with the `authenticated` profile, leaf by leaf, by `sanitizeStructured`. Payloads are not serialized, sanitized as one string, and re-parsed. Every string leaf passes through `redactText`, the same redaction function the text sanitizer uses, so the structural path is never weaker than the text path. Object keys are redacted too. A number that matches a sensitive pattern, such as a card number stored as a JSON number, is replaced by its redaction marker string.

A string leaf that holds a serialized object or array, such as Pi's `content[].text`, is parsed, sanitized recursively, and re-serialized with the producer's original indentation. Recursion into embedded JSON stops at a fixed depth, and a leaf past that depth is sanitized as plain text. Scalar-looking strings such as `"42"` stay strings.

The profile byte cap is enforced on the structure, not by cutting serialized text. The longest string leaves are shortened first, on a UTF-8 boundary, and end with `…[truncated]`. If the structure is still too large, tail items of the longest array are dropped. A structure that still does not fit is replaced by the `…[truncated]` marker string. Input that is not JSON-compatible, such as a cycle, a `bigint`, or a function, becomes a sanitized and truncated string, the same result the text path produces. Every record therefore re-parses as JSON. A property test (`packages/core/tests/sanitizer/structured.spec.ts`) checks both that the output re-parses and that the canary values it plants are redacted. The record-level format is described under [Tool-call records](diagnostics-and-audit.md#tool-call-records).

The text sanitizer's in-text URL pattern stops at a backslash. A URL inside JSON-escaped text therefore ends before an escaped quote (`\"`) instead of absorbing it. Before this change, absorbing the quote corrupted audit records and inflated the URL-rewrite counts.

### Stored secrets and trusted hosts

Workflow and tool payloads use typed references instead of literal stored credentials:

```yaml
kind: secret
key: shop.password
hosts:
  - shop.example.com
```

The value lives in the OS keychain under the `yantra` service. For a website fill, trusted host metadata must contain at least one host. Yantra compares that metadata with the browser's live host before resolving the secret. An exact host or a host under the same registrable domain is accepted; an unrelated host returns `SECRET_HOST_MISMATCH` before keychain access.

`browser_fill_element` is the only live agent tool that accepts a stored `secret_ref`. It requires confirmation, resolves the secret after the host check, skips suggestion and committed-value readback, and returns no secret value. It also performs no editee resolution: locating the control a page routed keystrokes into means searching every observed control for the value that was sent, which for a credential would be a readback of secret-derived state compared against the whole page, so that path is structurally unavailable to a secret fill rather than merely unused. `browser_fill_form` accepts only non-secret strings and never submits.

Resolution writes only the reference key, step, time, and `resolved`, `not_found`, or `error` outcome to `secrets.jsonl`. A semantic trace stores only the key. Explicit buffers are cleared after use on a best-effort basis, but JavaScript strings and runtime copies cannot be guaranteed to be erased from memory.

### Protected fields

Some page controls hold values that must never be read back into Yantra, whoever supplied them. A control is protected, and its contents are withheld from every read, for one of three reasons, checked in this order:

| Reason          | Applies when                                                                                                                                                                |
| --------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `password`      | The control is an `input[type="password"]`.                                                                                                                                 |
| `autocomplete`  | Its `autocomplete` attribute contains `current-password`, `new-password`, `one-time-code`, `cc-number`, `cc-csc`, or `cc-exp` as a whole token, matched case-insensitively. |
| `secret_marker` | It carries Yantra's `data-yantra-secret` attribute.                                                                                                                         |

Only these attribute facts decide it, never the control's value, label, or site. The observation reports a protected control with `value_present: true` when it holds anything and `withheld: <reason>` in place of `value`, so a control classified as protected by mistake is visible to the model and in the audit trail. Live observation and deterministic replay classify controls with the same reasons and the same token list. The in-page scan refuses to run when it is not given that token list, rather than fall back to disclosing every autocomplete-protected value it reaches.

A value sent to a protected control — a literal or a resolved `{{user:…}}` placeholder — is checked **inside the page**: the text that was sent is passed into the page, compared with what the control holds there, and only a verdict (`exact`, `reformatted`, `truncated`, `different`, or `empty`) and whether the control holds anything come back. Passing the sent text to the page is no new exposure, because the same text was just typed into it. The protected value is therefore not available to any result, failure detail, ledger record, log line, or message to record. A successful fill reports `withheld: { reason, verdict, ref }` in place of `committed`, and a failure reports `withheld` and the verdict as `match` in place of `observed`; see [Agentic Tasks](agentic-tasks.md#what-it-does).

A stored website secret stays blind. The `secret_ref` path keeps its host binding, confirmation, masking, and sensitive-screen latch, enters the value once with no readback and no in-page check, and its tool result is unchanged: no `committed` and no `withheld`. No stored secret is ever passed into the page as text to compare against.

### Consent and fail-closed behavior

Yantra requires a confirmation immediately before:

- clicks whose accessible name contains `buy`, `pay`, `purchase`, `book`, `order`, `submit`, `confirm`, or `place order`;
- a live `browser_fill_element` call using a stored `secret_ref`; and
- saved workflow steps explicitly marked `requires_confirmation`.

An attended, non-JSON TTY displays the action, host, summary, and consequence, then asks `Allow this action? [y/N]`. Only `y` or `yes` grants it; an empty answer denies. The wait is bounded by `--confirm-timeout` and the run's remaining wall-clock budget.

Denial, timeout, missing consent wiring, `--json`, or a non-TTY live agent run fails closed: the protected operation is not executed. The confirmation protocol records only `user_interactive`, `user_cli_confirm`, or `timeout` as decision provenance; there is no agent decision type.

Scheduled work uses pause-and-notify rather than auto-confirmation. For a genuinely parked run, `yantra confirm <run-id> grant|deny` appends the human decision. Continuing execution is a separate resume or daemon-poll step; the command itself does not execute the protected action.

### Engine-enforced no-submit

When a `do` goal says not to submit, the agent declares `effects.submit: "forbidden"` in its [task contract](agentic-tasks.md#task-contract), and the engine, not the model, then keeps the form unsubmitted. Once any contract revision forbids submitting, a later revision cannot allow it again.

Under `forbidden`, `browser_click` classifies its target before the confirmation gate and before any click. A target is submit-class when either signal fires:

- **Structural:** it is a native `<button>` whose resolved `type` is `submit` (which includes a `<button>` with no `type`), or an `<input type="submit">` or `<input type="image">`, **and** it has a form owner, including ownership through a `form=` attribute. A submit-typed button outside any form submits nothing and does not count.
- **Name:** its accessible name matches the protected-action lexicon used for confirmations (`buy`, `pay`, `purchase`, `book`, `order`, `submit`, `confirm`, or `place order`).

The structural facts come from one read-only evaluation of the element, which changes no page state. Both signals are generic DOM semantics; nothing is keyed to a site. A `type="button"` control, a `<button>` outside a form, and an element with an unrelated name click normally.

A submit-class click is refused with the non-retryable `SUBMIT_FORBIDDEN`, whose cause is `structural` or `name`. The refusal runs before the confirmation gate, so no confirmation request is built, no prompt appears, and no submission handler on the page fires. The message says the control was not clicked and why, and tells the agent to leave the form unsubmitted and continue with the remaining items or finish with `result_publish`.

A saved workflow could click on the agent's behalf, so under `forbidden`, `workflow_run` refuses before running any workflow whose plan, or a workflow it calls, contains a `click` step, with `SUBMIT_FORBIDDEN` and cause `nested-workflow`. The check is structural and runs nothing. It also refuses when it cannot rule a click out: a plan that cannot be loaded, a call with no callee, or more than 16 workflows to inspect. An extract-only workflow still runs.

Each refusal is recorded in the run's action ledger and as one `submit_refused` line in `runtime.jsonl` with the signal and bare hostname, never the control's name. At publication the contract's `effects.submit` requirement is met when no submit-class click executed, and refused attempts are counted in its reason. With `effects.submit: "allowed"`, the default, click and confirmation behavior is unchanged.

### Browser, URL, and web safety

The model receives a command-specific tool catalog. Application sessions contain no unrestricted shell, filesystem, code-editing, or arbitrary-network tools. `script_run` accepts only the registered first-party transformations `table_normalize`, `dedupe_lines`, and `json_pick`, with validated arguments and resource caps.

Outbound URL checks enforce absolute HTTP(S) URLs, HTTPS by default, a 2048-character limit, credential-shape scanning, optional `--allow-host` restrictions, and run-wide navigation/host budgets. `browser_navigate` and `web_fetch` add URL provenance: a user-supplied URL or host, search/fetch result, link a page read offered, visited page, redirect, or intercepted popup must attest the origin, path, and query-parameter names. Query values may vary on an attested path, but new paths, parameter names, or identifiers are refused with `URL_NOT_FROM_EVIDENCE`. See [Discovered-link provenance](#discovered-link-provenance).

The web ethics gate honors robots rules, blocklists, and rate limits. Bot walls and CAPTCHAs produce a refusal or handoff; there is no ignore or evasion flag; see [Challenge pages](#challenge-pages). `web_fetch` accepts only HTML or plain text and enforces streamed body-size limits. Browser popups are closed and surfaced for a later policy-checked navigation; JavaScript prompts are dismissed rather than silently accepted.

An agentic run also honors a scraped search provider's rate limiting. It asks a scraped provider one query at a time, each started at least 2 seconds after the previous one, and after that provider's first anti-bot challenge or rate-limit refusal it asks it nothing more for the rest of the run: later searches return `SEARCH_BLOCKED` with cause `circuit-open` without contacting the provider. Nothing rotates the user agent, proxies the request, or changes the browser's fingerprint to get past a refusal, and the run does not switch to another provider.

Agent browser profiles are fresh and ephemeral by default. They are removed on normal completion, abort, or browser teardown. Persistent logged-in agent profiles are not part of this surface. The background pages an agentic run uses for scraped search results and fetch fallbacks each get their own isolated browser context, closed when that read ends. No cookie, storage, or cache entry from one background read is visible to the next, and none of them shares state with the task browser's page.

### Discovered-link provenance

A page read offers links, and a link it offers is something the run may follow. Without that, a model that cannot reach a page through the tools assembles the URL itself, and a guessed URL that resolves to plausible but wrong data is a correctness hole. Provenance is the boundary between the two.

- **What is recorded.** Every URL an agentic page read shows the model is recorded as `discovered`, naming the evidence ID of the page that offered it and how it was offered: a link in `links[]` (with its kind, such as `facet` or `pagination`), a record's URL or secondary link, an absolute URL property in structured data, or a URL written in returned text. A URL the model was not shown, such as a link trimmed by a size bound or one inside a hidden part of the page, is never recorded. The first attestation of a URL is the one kept.
- **What is offered.** A URL is offered only when the model-visible transform, which applies user-input masking and then the `public` sanitizer, leaves it byte-identical, so the URL the model copies is exactly the URL that was recorded. Any other URL is shown as `url: null`, counted in `coverage.links.withheld`, and not recorded. `javascript:`, `data:`, `mailto:`, `tel:`, and same-document links are never offered, and a page offers at most 40 links.
- **What the goal attests.** A URL the user typed in the goal is attested exactly as written. A hostname the user typed without a scheme, such as `Use example.com`, attests only that site's origin roots, `https://example.com/` and `http://example.com/`: no path below the root and no `www.` variant. A hostname that is part of an email address (`alice@example.com`) or of a typed URL attests nothing extra. Production URL policy still requires HTTPS, so the `http` root matters only on a loopback test host. A false positive such as `node.js` grants only a root navigation that fails. Only the user's raw goal and `--allow-host` are read; a task contract's `required_sources`, which the model writes, attests nothing.
- **What stays refused.** `web_fetch` and `browser_navigate` refuse a URL that no search result, page read, goal, or `--allow-host` entry attested with `URL_NOT_FROM_EVIDENCE`. The refusal happens before URL policy, the run's document store, or any budget is consulted, so nothing is fetched and nothing is charged. Because `web_fetch` is gated too, a guessed URL cannot be fetched first and then navigated to as if a fetch had attested it.
- **What a discovered link does not bypass.** Provenance only grants permission to try. A discovered URL still passes the unchanged URL policy (length cap, HTTPS, credential-shape scan, and host budget) and the ethics gate.
- **The audit chain.** `web_fetch` and `browser_navigate` records in `tool-calls.jsonl` carry a `provenance` detail on success, on a provenance refusal, and on a policy or site failure: `match` (`exact`, `origin-root`, `query-variant`, `allowed-host`, or `none`), `kind` (`goal`, `allow-host`, `tool`, `discovered`, or `none`), and for a discovered URL `via`, the evidence ID of the page that offered it, and `link_kind`. That page's own fetch record states how its URL was attested in turn, so a chain of hops can be reconstructed back to the goal or a search result. The detail carries IDs and kinds only, never page text, and is never shown to the model.

Structured data is untrusted, bounded input. Schema.org JSON-LD is `JSON.parse`d and never evaluated. Each script is read up to 256 KiB and all scripts up to 1 MiB in total; a block that is larger or fails to parse is counted in coverage rather than read. An entity is returned only when its type is in a hand-maintained allowlist of schema.org vocabulary names (`Product`, `Offer`, `AggregateOffer`, `ItemList`, `Organization`, `Place`, `Event`, and listed subtypes of them); other types are listed in `coverage.structured.ignored_types`. Each entity is flattened to at most 40 properties, nesting depth 4, 300 characters per string, and 2 KB in total, and a page returns at most 25 entities. Every string reaches the model through the same sanitizer as page text, so phone and email redaction applies to structured data too. Microdata is read under the same allowlist and bounds.

Extraction is structural only. The page analyzer never reads a `class` or `id` attribute, never names a host, and never branches on a URL literal, and a boundary test enforces it.

### Challenge pages

Yantra classifies every response it fetches before anything extracts it, so a human-verification page is never read as content and never becomes a source. This applies to agentic `web_fetch` and `web_search` reads, to the live-page snapshot `browser_extract` analyzes for every kind except `content`, and to the deterministic `ask --no-llm` and `research --no-llm` pipelines, which share the same fetcher.

Classification uses a short, documented list of generic challenge-widget markers. Every entry is a standard component that human-verification widgets render with, or a phrase their interstitials show. No site, host, or brand appears in it.

- Widget markers: a `data-sitekey` attribute; a `g-recaptcha`, `h-captcha`, or `cf-turnstile` class or id; and a `captcha` token in the `id`, `class`, or `name` of a `<form>` or of an element inside one.
- Phrases, matched in the page's `<title>` or first `<h1>`: "verify you are human", "are you a robot", "unusual traffic", "checking your browser", "press and hold", and "complete the security check".

The check is a single lowercase text scan of the HTML already fetched, and the page is parsed only when that scan finds one of those tokens. A response that is not HTML is never a challenge. A parsed page is a challenge when any of these holds, where visible text excludes `script`, `style`, `noscript`, and `template` content:

1. a widget marker is present and the visible text is under 1,500 characters;
2. a phrase is in the `<title>` or first `<h1>` and the visible text is under 3,000 characters;
3. a phrase is in the `<title>` or first `<h1>` and a widget marker is present, at any size.

The size limits keep a long article that embeds a comment-form CAPTCHA, or an article about CAPTCHAs, from being treated as a challenge. Rule 3 requires both independent signals together, which is how an interstitial padded with help text is still recognized.

What happens next is the policy the user signed off on for this feature (policy b):

- When Yantra's HTTP client, which identifies itself as `YantraBot`, receives a challenge page, the URL is rendered **once** in the standard headless browser. Nothing about that browser's identity is changed, and there is no solving, waiting for the challenge to clear, or retry.
- A challenge page in that render, or in any browser render a fetch escalated to, is terminal for the URL. The page is never extracted. Agentic `web_fetch` returns the non-retryable `SITE_CHALLENGE` with `handoff: true`, so a run that publishes nothing ends as a user handoff, and the run never requests that URL again. A `web_search` hit, or a deterministic source, becomes a `blocked` failure with reason `challenge page (<marker>)`.
- A live page the agent has already navigated to is checked the same way before `browser_extract` analyzes it for any kind other than `content`. A challenge there returns `SITE_CHALLENGE` with `handoff: true`, and the page is not analyzed, recorded as evidence, or used to attest any link.
- In an agentic run, both tiers are audited in `runtime.jsonl`: a `fetch_challenge` warning names the tier, the marker ID, and the bare host, and a `fetch_escalated` line records the single render. The published document discloses both outcomes: a `blocked` notice for each host whose browser render was a challenge, and an `other` notice for each host that challenged only the HTTP client before its page was read in the browser.

### Context grants and local personalization

Every model-backed agent run receives current date, timezone, and locale from the host environment. Those facts are always supplied. User location is different: `context.location` gates a sanitized value composed from approved `locale.city` and `locale.region` preferences.

Denied and unconfigured location both appear to the model as `not available`. A self-referential goal such as “hotels near me” fails before provider or browser work when no location is available, with exit code `4`; Yantra does not infer a city from the timezone.

Personalization sends only a short, sanitized summary built from approved preferences. Operational `agent.*` settings and raw run history are not personalization context. Machine-learned values require explicit approval before they can contribute.

### Screenshots and local captures

Yantra has two screenshot tools with separate authority, and the grant applies to only one of them.

- **Vision Assist (`browser_screenshot`)** sends raw, unmasked pixels to the model provider. It needs the stored `context.screenshots: true` grant and an image-capable model; see [Opt-In Vision Assist](vision-assist.md).
- **Deliverable capture (`browser_capture`)** saves a clean PNG that the user asked for and never sends it. It needs no grant: `context.screenshots` governs model transmission only, and nothing reads, writes, or infers that grant for a local capture. Its result returns no image content, and the tool middleware still accepts image content only from an available `browser_screenshot` call, so a `browser_capture` result carrying an image is refused. The model receives only paths, dimensions, byte sizes, and labels, never the pixels or a SHA-256.

A local capture keeps the protections a capture needs:

- **Secret latch.** Filling a stored website secret latches the current document against capture. `browser_capture` checks the latch before reserving budget or taking any pixels, and refuses with `SCREENSHOT_SENSITIVE_SCREEN` (cause `secret-latched`), the same code Vision Assist uses. If the latch cannot be read, the capture is refused too. The latch clears only when a new top-level document loads.
- **No Yantra marks.** It refuses with `CAPTURE_UNAVAILABLE` (cause `overlay-present`) while Vision Assist's marks overlay is on the page, so a saved picture never shows Yantra's labels. It also discards a capture whose page moved to a new document during the capture.
- **Owner-only files, all or nothing.** Files are written under `screenshots/` at mode `0600` inside a `0700` directory, each through a temporary file renamed into place. A failure partway through a call removes the files that call had already written.
- **Its own budget.** At most 4 calls per run, 6 files per call, 1,920 x 4,096 px and 8 MiB per file, and 40 MiB per run, all checked before anything is written. Vision Assist's budget is separate and unchanged.
- **Audit.** Every file is recorded in `tool-calls.jsonl` as a metadata-only artifact reference with `sent_to_model: false`. `yantra audit` lists it under `Saved captures (kept on this computer, never sent to the model):`, separately from `The model saw these images:`. The raw-session warning appears only for images the model saw; see [Audit and report views](diagnostics-and-audit.md#audit-and-report-views).

`--no-screenshots` works only downward. It removes both capture tools for one run and can never add one. A model-authored task contract grants nothing either: declaring a screenshot in `artifacts` cannot register `browser_screenshot`, change the Vision Assist gate, or bypass the latch. Both capture decisions are recorded before the first tool call, with the reasons any tool is off, in `manifest.json` (`agent.capture`) and `run-health.json` (`capture`). `browser_capture` exists only in agentic sessions. Replay, scheduled runs, and nested workflows never register it.

### Audit records and sensitive local artifacts

Each run has a local directory under `<yantra-data-dir>/runs/<run-id>/`. Depending on the path taken, it can contain:

| Artifact                                             | Safety-relevant contents                                                                                                                                                                     |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `manifest.json`                                      | Outcome, scope summary, model/provider and prompt/tool provenance; credential source but never credential value                                                                              |
| `tool-calls.jsonl`                                   | Ordered input/output projections sanitized leaf by leaf, status, error code, duration, and confirmation linkage                                                                              |
| `secrets.jsonl`                                      | Secret reference keys and resolution outcomes only                                                                                                                                           |
| `confirmations.jsonl`                                | Requested action/host/description/cost/consequence and human decision provenance                                                                                                             |
| `trace.json`                                         | Successful browser actions with marked placeholders or secret keys, not resolved values                                                                                                      |
| `captures/`                                          | Oversized sanitized web/browser extraction payloads                                                                                                                                          |
| `screenshots/`                                       | Raw, unmasked PNG pixels from Vision Assist (sent to the model) and `browser_capture` (kept locally), owner-only; sensitive local material                                                   |
| `contract.json`                                      | The declared task contract, written only after every string passed the `public` sanitizer and control characters were stripped; its action `requirements` hold ids and revision numbers only |
| `agent/<session>.jsonl`                              | Raw provider-session format containing the model-visible conversation and model responses; sensitive local material                                                                          |
| `report.md`, `brief.*`, `events.jsonl`, `usage.json` | Human report, published result, lifecycle, and usage data                                                                                                                                    |

Runtime-derived Brief notices carry no untrusted text. Notices that Yantra attaches to a published result for search failures, exhausted budgets, challenge pages, and per-source read failures are built only from fixed phrase tables, counts, stable error codes, and bare hostnames. They never include page text or provider text. A per-source failure reason that is not one of the known stable phrases, which could contain a URL, is replaced by a stable phrase such as `fetch failed`. The same ledger produces `run-health.json` and the report's Run Health section, which are described in [Run Health](diagnostics-and-audit.md#run-health).

Operator diagnostics in the runtime log carry closed fields only. A `tool_failure` line has a tool name, error code, cause, provider name, bare hostname, and budget limit. A `fetch_challenge` line has the tier, a closed marker ID, and a bare hostname; a `fetch_escalated` line has the escalation reason and a bare hostname; a `search_breaker_open` line has the provider name and a closed cause. A `run_health` line holds the run-health summary. A `contract_declared` line has the revision, the deliverable, field and filter counts, the required sources as bare hostnames, the fill coverage, the artifact count, and the submit term, never the subject, field, filter, or note text. An `action_recorded` line has the entry kind, sequence number, document epoch, and bare hostname, plus a closed count, signal, or scope; a `submit_refused` line has the signal and bare hostname; a `fulfillment_evaluated` line has per-status counts only. None of them carries a field name, control name, typed value, or path. The action ledger behind them keeps sanitized field and control names in memory for the run's evaluation and never a typed value, selector, or secret reference. A `cause` is accepted only as a closed token: no whitespace, at most 80 characters from `A–Z`, `a–z`, `0–9`, `_`, `.`, `:`, and `-`. Any other cause is dropped, and a token derived from the error code is used instead. A host that is not hostname-shaped is dropped. The runtime-log safety assertions in `@yantra/test-helpers` reject a `cause` that is not such a token or that contains `//`.

`yantra audit <run-id>` is read-only. It renders the structured manifest, tool-call, confirmation, secret-reference, event, and usage projections; it does not parse the raw provider session. An incomplete start record is shown as incomplete rather than treated as success.

## How to Use It

### Protect one-off input

Use single quotes in bash, zsh, and PowerShell so the shell does not interpolate the goal:

```bash
yantra do 'sign in as @username{u1} with @password{p1}' --allow-host xyz.com
```

For `cmd.exe`, use double quotes:

```bat
yantra do "sign in as @username{u1} with @password{p1}" --allow-host xyz.com
```

Yantra deliberately does not use `${...}` because bash and PowerShell expand it inside double quotes before Yantra can protect it. Markers do not hide command-line arguments from shell history, the terminal process, the operating system, or other local software that can inspect process arguments.

`do`, `ask`, and `research` each print the goal as received to stderr as `goal: "<text>"`, so you can see when the shell rewrote it. Before printing, this goal echo replaces credential-shaped and `@{...}`-marked values with their placeholders, the same way the run sees them. It also removes control characters and escapes quotes and backslashes. A goal with a malformed `@{...}` marker is never printed. In its place the echo reads `goal: [not shown: the goal has a malformed @{...} marker]`, because an unclosed marker may hold a secret. The goal echo goes only to stderr, so `--json` stdout is unchanged.

Values of eight or more characters are echo-masked wherever they occur. Shorter values are masked only at token boundaries to avoid corrupting unrelated text. A marked value under three characters produces an advisory warning in human-readable output because a site can embed it inside a longer token; warnings are suppressed under JSON output. Ingress protection still applies regardless of length.

Model-backed `do` always uses this ingress. `ask` and `research` use it on their model-backed path. Their `--no-llm` pipelines open no provider session and do not use model-placeholder resolution; do not add marker syntax to a deterministic search term expecting it to be stripped automatically.

### Control location and personalization

```bash
yantra prefs set locale.city "Naperville, IL"
yantra prefs set locale.region US
yantra prefs set context.location false
yantra prefs set context.location true
yantra prefs set personalization.enabled false
yantra prefs list
yantra prefs --forget locale.city
```

`yantra init` collects the initial location grant only on an interactive TTY when it is writing a new or reset profile. `--yes`, `--json`, non-TTY use, and an unchanged existing profile do not prompt.

### Constrain a live browser run

Repeat `--allow-host` to name every host the run may use:

```bash
yantra do 'complete the public demo form' \
  --allow-host forms.example.com \
  --confirm-timeout 2m
```

An allowlisted host grants navigation within that user-named host; it does not weaken HTTPS, credential-shape, ethics, budget, or secret-host-binding checks.

### Resolve and inspect consent

Interactive consent happens inline. For a parked run:

```bash
yantra confirm <run-id> grant
yantra resume <run-id>

# Or deny it permanently:
yantra confirm <run-id> deny
```

Inspect the resulting trail in human-readable or structured form:

```bash
yantra audit <run-id>
yantra audit <run-id> --json
```

### Use durable website credentials

Saved workflows declare secret references such as `{{ secret:shop.password }}` rather than literal credentials. Populate the keychain with `yantra secret set <key>`, which reads the value from an echo-disabled prompt or piped stdin and rejects a positional value so the credential never reaches shell history or a process listing. Website fills additionally require trusted-host metadata: the secret reference carries a `hosts` list naming the sites allowed to receive that credential, and a fill into any other host is refused. Do not work around any of this by placing credentials in workflow YAML, params, outputs, or URLs.

See [Saved Workflows](saved-workflows.md) for workflow syntax and replay behavior.

## Inputs and Outputs

### User-visible inputs

| Input                          | Constraint or effect                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `@{...}` / `@tag{...}`         | Run-scoped masking for model-backed agent input; 1–2048 non-whitespace characters                            |
| `--allow-host <host>`          | Repeatable outbound-host restriction for `do`                                                                |
| `--confirm-timeout <duration>` | Maximum live confirmation wait; also bounded by remaining run time                                           |
| `--auth-secret <ref>`          | Runtime-only **model-provider key** reference; separate from website secrets                                 |
| `context.location`             | Grants or withholds the configured user location                                                             |
| `context.screenshots`          | Allows Vision Assist to send raw, unmasked screenshots to the model provider; not needed for a local capture |
| `--no-screenshots`             | Removes both capture tools for one `do`, `ask`, or `research` run; never adds one                            |
| `personalization.enabled`      | Enables or disables approved preference summary injection                                                    |
| `requires_confirmation`        | Saved-workflow action checkpoint on supported mutating verbs                                                 |

### Common safety outcomes

| Outcome                                                                     | Meaning                                                                                      |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Exit `1`                                                                    | Invalid marker, host, preference, workflow, or other validation failure                      |
| Exit `2`                                                                    | Execution, policy, or budget failure                                                         |
| Exit `3`                                                                    | Environment failure such as unavailable model authorization or required runtime service      |
| Exit `4`                                                                    | Human handoff, including denied/timed-out workflow confirmation or missing required location |
| `SECRET_HOST_MISMATCH`                                                      | Stored website secret was requested on an unrelated live host                                |
| `FILL_VALUE_INVALID`                                                        | A credential-shaped literal or invalid semantic fill was refused before mutation             |
| `CONFIRMATION_DENIED` / `CONFIRMATION_TIMEOUT` / `CONFIRMATION_UNAVAILABLE` | The protected action was not executed                                                        |
| `SUBMIT_FORBIDDEN`                                                          | The contract forbids submitting, so a submit-class click or clicking workflow was not run    |
| `URL_NOT_FROM_EVIDENCE`                                                     | A fetch or browser navigation used a URL, path, or parameter name nothing attested           |
| `URL_CREDENTIAL_SHAPE` / `URL_HOST_NOT_ALLOWED`                             | Outbound URL was refused by policy                                                           |
| `ETHICS_BLOCKED`                                                            | Robots, blocklist, or rate-limit policy refused the fetch or action                          |
| `SITE_CHALLENGE`                                                            | The page was a human-verification challenge in the standard browser; it was not read         |
| `SCREENSHOT_SENSITIVE_SCREEN`                                               | A stored secret was filled on this document, so no screenshot of it was taken or saved       |
| `CAPTURE_UNAVAILABLE`                                                       | A local capture could not be taken cleanly or within bounds; nothing was saved               |
| `SEARCH_BLOCKED` with cause `circuit-open`                                  | The search provider challenged or rate-limited an earlier query, so this search was not sent |

Expected failures are returned to the model as bounded, structured, retry-classified results. Unexpected exceptions are genericized in model-visible output.

## Configuration and Permissions

- Yantra-owned configuration uses one platform-independent home: `YANTRA_HOME` when that environment variable is non-empty, otherwise `~/.yantra`. The root contains `config.yaml`, `profile.yaml`, `blocklist.yaml`, and `sanitizer-hosts.yaml`; only the data and cache roots are independently relocatable. `profile.yaml` stores user-editable preferences, grants, and operational defaults, and must not contain website or provider credential values.
- The sanitizer host-override loader reads `<home>/sanitizer-hosts.yaml` by default, validates its versioned host mappings, and uses them for host matching. If the file is absent, it falls back to the packaged defaults; malformed YAML, invalid entries, and other read failures are reported instead of silently replacing the active rules. Reloading rereads the active file.
- The OS keychain stores model/search credentials and workflow secret values. If keychain support is unavailable, Yantra uses a degraded provider: reads report missing values and write/delete operations fail.
- Browser access is command-profiled: `ask` has web tools only; `research` also has read-only browsing (`browser_navigate`, `browser_observe`, `browser_extract`, never click or fill) unless the `agent.research_browse` preference is `false` or the run passes `--no-browse`; only `do` receives browser mutation tools. Nothing in the environment changes a catalog. A goal that needs clicks or fills in `research` is reported with `yantra do` named as the next step.
- The `task_contract` tool grants no authority: it writes no URL provenance, allowlist entry, budget, or screenshot grant, and a requested screenshot registers no capture tool. Its text is sanitized with the `public` profile, with marked user values masked back to placeholders and control characters stripped, before it is persisted, echoed to the terminal, or logged.
- Date, timezone, and locale are always model-visible in model-backed runs. Location is visible only when granted and configured. A granted preference or marked value sent to a website is disclosed to that website when the requested tool action uses it.
- With a remote model provider, sanitized prompts, tool results, and model-visible context leave the machine for that provider. Choosing a local provider changes that transport boundary; it does not disable Yantra's local sanitization and policy checks.

## Verification

The current safety envelope is exercised by no-LLM sanitizer, marker-parser, secret resolver, host-binding, scope-enforcer, confirmation, middleware, URL-policy, location-gate, audit, protocol, CLI, and browser-fill tests. `pnpm security:static-check` also checks recognized sanitize-before-send sites, SDK/package boundaries, and that raw index-history modules are unreachable from the configured LLM-payload assembly entrypoints.

A real-Chrome `do` scenario in `e2e/agent-do.spec.ts` fills a password and a card-number field from marked goal values and a third password from a host-bound stored secret, then byte-scans the model-visible tool results and every run-directory file outside the raw provider session, `tool-calls.jsonl`, `trace.json`, and `manifest.json` among them, for the synthetic values and the stored-secret canary, and requires zero hits.

The focused verification for this document passed 249 tests across 19 files, plus the static check over 678 TypeScript files. The live CLI help for `do`, `ask`, `research`, `confirm`, `audit`, and `prefs` was also checked.

## Limitations

- Explicit markers guarantee separation inside Yantra's model-prompt and persisted-artifact paths. They do not protect shell history, process arguments, terminal capture, swap/crash dumps, browser/page recipients, or other privileged local software.
- Marker tags control privacy labeling, not authorization. A marked password is not automatically host-bound or confirmation-gated. Use a stored website secret for those properties, and use `--allow-host` to narrow one-off work.
- Keyword and PII/credential shape detection is best-effort and intentionally conservative. It cannot identify every person's name, address, account number, national identifier, or arbitrary secret, and it can produce false positives or negatives.
- Echo masking for values under eight characters is boundary-aware; an under-three-character value embedded inside a larger token may reappear in returned page text. Marked ingress remains protected, but avoid very short protected values when possible.
- `read-only-data` deliberately bypasses PII stripping so a model can reason over real values. Use it only when that disclosure is intended; its protection is static action restriction, not secrecy from the model provider.
- Buffer clearing is best-effort. V8 can intern or copy JavaScript strings, so Yantra does not claim guaranteed memory zeroing.
- Challenge detection covers only the documented generic markers and phrases. A human-verification page that shows none of them is not recognized and is treated as ordinary content. A page that returns HTTP 200 with "not found" text is not a challenge either.
- URL provenance gates the agentic `web_fetch` and `browser_navigate` tools only. The deterministic `ask --no-llm` and `research --no-llm` pipelines fetch the URLs their own search returns and are not provenance gated.
- Provenance attests that a page offered a URL, not that the URL is safe or relevant. A discovered link is still subject to URL policy and the ethics gate, and its content is untrusted data like any other page.
- A link the sanitizer would alter, for example one whose path contains a masked user value, is withheld rather than offered, so it cannot be followed even when the page plainly links to it.
- Heuristic confirmation covers named protected clicks, stored-secret fills, and explicitly flagged workflow steps. It cannot infer every consequential action from arbitrary site wording. Mark critical workflow actions with `requires_confirmation`.
- Engine-enforced no-submit recognizes native submit controls with a form owner and names in the protected-action lexicon. A control that submits only through page script, such as a `div` with `role="button"` and an unrelated name, is not recognized as submit-class.
- Non-interactive live agent confirmations fail closed rather than creating a generally resumable pending prompt. `yantra confirm` operates only on a request that was actually parked, and recording a grant is separate from resuming or polling the run.
- The run directory and raw provider session are sensitive local data. Restrictive permissions are best-effort on Windows. `yantra audit` intentionally avoids the raw session, but anyone with filesystem access can open it. Treat debug/process logs as sensitive too; model-visible error genericization is not a guarantee about every local diagnostic sink.
- A saved capture is never sent to the model, but it is still raw, unmasked pixels of whatever the page showed, written to the run directory. Treat `screenshots/` with the same care as the rest of the run directory. The secret latch covers stored website secrets only. A value typed from a goal marker is not latched, so a capture taken after such a fill can show it if the page displays it.
- Ephemeral browser-profile cleanup runs on normal teardown paths, but no application can guarantee cleanup after abrupt machine loss or external process termination. Persistent authenticated agent profiles are not supported.
- `script_run` executes trusted registered first-party code in a Node worker. The worker supplies resource containment, not an OS security sandbox for untrusted code.

For adjacent workflows, see [Profiles, Preferences, History, and Ambient Context](profiles-and-history.md), [Agentic Tasks with `yantra do`](agentic-tasks.md), [Diagnostics, Audit, and Run Inspection](diagnostics-and-audit.md), the [architecture](../architecture.md), and the [usage guide](../usage.md).
